title: The tiger raised
hook: a student with a spell revives a dead tiger, which kills him (Jataka 150)
tomorrow: The donkey in the lion's skin

segments.voice: Yesterday, a prince walked through a forest of yakkhini, without turning his head. Your line was don't look back. Did you walk past something? Today, a spell, and a tiger. Day eight hundred twenty-nine.

A spell for raising the dead. That's what a young student named Sanjiva has picked up from his teacher. Only half of it, though: the words that bring a body back to life, and not the words that would undo them. One day he's out in the forest with the other students, gathering wood, and they come across a dead tiger lying in the grass. Sanjiva has an idea. His friends have a different one. Today, the tiger raised.
screen: `HALF A SPELL.` → `A DEAD TIGER IN THE GRASS.` → `SANJIVA HAS AN IDEA.`

segments.voice: First, the half-learned spell. The tale says Sanjiva knew the charm for raising the dead but had never learned the charm for putting them down again. He has the start of something and no way to finish it. Second, the boast. He tells his friends he'll bring the tiger back to life. They don't quite believe him, but they aren't foolish either. Before he begins, they climb up into the trees. Third, the waking. Sanjiva says the words. The tiger stirs, rises, and the first thing it does is spring at the man who woke it. It kills him on the spot, and the tale says the tiger fell dead right there beside him. His friends come down from the branches and carry the news home. Fourth, the teacher's verse. The teacher, the Buddha in an earlier life, hears what happened and gives the tale its lesson: whoever helps a wicked one back to his feet is harmed by him, just as the tiger killed the one who raised it. The frame of the story is about a king who took a schemer as his friend, so the warning first of all concerns companions. But the picture reaches further than that. Some things in a life are lying still for good reason: an old grudge, a habit that nearly sank you, an argument that finally went quiet. The words that wake them are easy to say. Putting them down again is the half of the spell that's easy to skip.
screen: `HALF A SPELL.` · `FRIENDS CLIMB THE TREES.` · `THE TIGER WAKES AND SPRINGS.` · `DON'T RAISE THE WICKED.` · then, large: `CAREFUL WHAT YOU REVIVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit, and let the mind wander a little, and watch what it tries to wake. An old argument. A grudge. A craving that had gone quiet. You'll know it when it stirs. Don't say the words that bring it to its feet. See it lying there, and leave it in the grass. Come back to the breath. Later today, before you reopen something that's been still, pause once and ask: do I know how to put this down again? The bell holds the time.
Sanjiva. The student with half a spell, who revived a dead tiger in a Jataka tale, and was killed by it. Today's word.
Your line: careful what you revive. Today, before you bring back an old quarrel or an old habit, ask whether you know the other half of the spell. Day eight hundred twenty-nine.

screen: `DAY 829 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE DONKEY IN THE LION'S SKIN.`

howItsDone: Jataka tales are retold in Buddhist sermons and children's classes, and a retelling often closes on the tale's verse, here the teacher's warning about whom we help back to their feet.

match.prompt: the tiger raised: tap the pairs.

myth: Sanjiva knew how to put the tiger back down
he learned the spell to raise the dead, not the one to undo it.
his friends climbed trees before he spoke the spell
they didn't quite believe him, but they weren't taking chances.
the tiger walked off into the forest
it killed Sanjiva and fell dead beside him.

fork.setup: you're one of the students. Sanjiva says he's going to raise the dead tiger. what do you do?
options: cheer him on from close by.
help him drag it into the open.
fork.reveal: the friends climbed the trees, and lived. the tiger woke and killed the one who raised it.

trapdoor: what you thought: a spooky story about magic gone wrong.
what it means: some things are better left lying still; raising what is harmful harms the one who raises it.
what a scholar hears: the tale's frame is about a king who befriended a schemer, so the teacher's verse warns first about the company we keep.

notes: Jataka 150 paraphrased: Sanjiva knows the spell to raise the dead but not the counter-spell; friends climb trees; the revived tiger kills him and falls dead on the spot; the Bodhisatta-teacher's verse warns against helping the wicked. Confirm.
Frame (King Ajatasattu's friendship with Devadatta) is described only as 'a king who took a schemer as his friend'; confirm wording is fair.
